title: الجمل الشرطية المتقدمة / Advanced conditional sentences
bridge: In Spanish, mixed conditionals combine tenses to express hypothetical situations with consequences in another time. In Arabic, the structure is notably different: there is no direct equivalent of the compound conditional (habría hecho), and particles such as لو (law) are used for counterfactual hypotheses and إن (in) for real or possible conditions. The verb after لو often appears in the past tense, even when referring to the present or future, which often confuses Spanish speakers. Additionally, the response to a condition with لو is introduced with لـ (la) + a verb in the past or present, depending on the temporal nuance.
rule: In Arabic, there are two main types of conditionals: real (with إن / idha) and counterfactual (with لو). For mixed conditionals, لو + past tense verb is used for the condition, and the apodosis (result) may be in the past or present depending on whether the consequence refers to the past or present/future. The particle لـ (la) is placed before the verb in the apodosis for counterfactual responses. Furthermore, if the condition is negative, لو لم (law lam) + past tense verb is used. It is important to note that neither the subjunctive nor the conditional mood is used in Arabic; instead, past and present tenses are employed with specific particles. To express an unreal wish, ليت (layta) + subjunctive or perfect is used.

concept_examples.text: لو كنت مكانه، لما فعلت ذلك.
concept_examples.translation: If I were in his place, I wouldn’t have done that.
concept_examples.phonetic: law kuntu makānahu, lamā faʿaltu dhālika.

concept_examples.text: إن درست جيدًا، ستنجح في الامتحان.
concept_examples.translation: If you study well, you will pass the exam.
concept_examples.phonetic: in darasta jayyidan, satanjaḥu fī al-imtiḥān.

concept_examples.text: لو لم تكن مريضًا، لسافرت معنا.
concept_examples.translation: If you hadn’t been sick, you would have traveled with us.
concept_examples.phonetic: law lam takun marīḍan, lasāfarta maʿanā.

concept_examples.text: لو كنت أعرف رقمه، لاتصلت به الآن.
concept_examples.translation: If I knew his number, I would call him right now.
concept_examples.phonetic: law kuntu aʿrifu raqmahu, la-ttaṣaltu bihi al-āna.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, we use 'habría' or 'haría' for the consequence of a counterfactual conditional. In Arabic, the apodosis of a condition with لو must be preceded by the particle لـ (la), not سـ (sa-) which indicates the future. Although Spanish uses 'te habría dicho' or 'te diría', in Arabic the past tense with لـ is typically used: لأخبرتك. The error comes from translating 'habría' literally as a conditional auxiliary, which does not exist in Arabic.

examples.translation: If you study, you pass.
examples.note: In Arabic, real conditions with إن usually use both verbs in the present tense (indicative), even though Spanish may use the future.

examples.translation: If you return, I will help you.
examples.note: The apodosis can include the future particle سـ (sa-) to indicate a future consequence.

examples.original: لو كنت غنيًا، لسافرت حول العالم.
examples.phonetic: law kuntu ghanīyan, lasāfartu ḥawla al-ʿālam.
examples.translation: If I were rich, I would travel around the world.
examples.note: Here the condition is unreal in the present, but the apodosis is expressed with past + لـ, not present as in Spanish.

examples.original: لو درست أكثر، لنجحت العام الماضي.
examples.phonetic: law darasta akthar, lanajaḥta al-ʿām al-māḍī.
examples.translation: If you had studied more, you would have passed last year.
examples.note: Mixed conditional: condition in the past (unrealized hypothesis) and consequence also in the past. The particle لـ is mandatory in the apodosis.

examples.translation: If it hadn’t rained, we would have gone out.
examples.note: The negation of the condition is formed with لو لم + past tense verb. The apodosis takes لـ + past.

examples.original: لو لا الجو، لذهبنا إلى الشاطئ.
examples.phonetic: law lā al-jawwu, la-dhahabnā ilā al-shāṭiʾ.
examples.translation: If it weren’t for the weather, we would go to the beach.
examples.note: لو لا is used with a noun or pronoun to express 'if it weren’t for...' (present unreal) or 'if it hadn’t been for...' (past unreal).

examples.original: لو كنت تعيش هنا، لاستمتعت بالشمس.
examples.phonetic: law kutta taʿīsh hunā, la-stamtaʿta bil-shams.
examples.translation: If you lived here, you would enjoy the sun.
examples.note: Mixed conditional in the present: condition with لو + past, apodosis with لـ + past, but referring to the present.

title: المبني للمجهول: صيغ متقدمة / Advanced Passive Voice
bridge: In Spanish, the passive voice is formed with 'ser + past participle' and sometimes with 'se'. In Arabic, the passive is expressed mainly by changing the internal vowels of the verb, without needing an auxiliary verb. This can be confusing because the sentence structure changes: the agent is not mentioned, and the verb agrees with the subject, which is the patient. Arabic does not have a direct equivalent to the passive with 'se' or to passive constructions with modals used in Spanish; to express passive possibility, constructions with 'صيغة المفعول' or verbs like 'يُمكِن' are used.
rule: In Arabic, the passive voice is formed by altering the short vowels of the verb. For the past tense: the first vowel becomes 'u' and the last 'i' (for example, كَتَبَ → كُتِبَ). For the present tense: the first vowel becomes 'u' and the penultimate vowel becomes 'a' (for example, يَكْتُبُ → يُكْتَبُ). The agent is not mentioned, and the grammatical subject (patient) agrees with the verb in gender and number. In compound forms (gerunds, infinitives, modals), constructions such as 'يَجِبُ + أنْ + فعل مبني للمجهول' or 'يُمْكِنُ + أنْ + فعل مبني للمجهول' are used. For gerunds and infinitives, the 'مصدر' with passive meaning or structures like 'بعدَ أنْ يُكتَب' are used.

concept_examples.translation: The book was written.
The lesson is written every day.
This can be said in Arabic.

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because the student translates the Spanish passive directly using the active structure with the agent mentioned. In Arabic, the passive is indicated only by the vowel change, and the agent is not mentioned. To form the passive correctly, change the verb's vowels and omit the agent.

examples.translation: The book was read.
examples.note: Observe the vowel change: from قَرَأَ to قُرِئَ. The subject (الكتاب) is masculine and singular, so the verb ends in -a.

examples.translation: The letter was written.
examples.note: The ending -at indicates that the subject (الرسالة) is feminine.

examples.translation: The door is opened.
examples.note: In the present tense, the first vowel becomes 'u' and the penultimate 'a' (يَفْتَحُ → يُفْتَحُ).

examples.translation: The lessons are written.
examples.note: When the subject is feminine or plural non-human, 'tu' is used instead of 'yu'.

levels.label: التعبير عن الاحتمال والوجوب
levels.translation: Expressing possibility and obligation in passive voice

examples.translation: This matter must be resolved.
examples.note: The structure 'يجب + أنْ + passive present verb' is used. The verb 'يُحَلَّ' is passive.

examples.translation: The movie can be watched tonight.
examples.note: For possibility, 'يمكن + أنْ + passive verb' is used.

title: الخطاب المنقول المتقدم / Advanced reported speech
bridge: In Spanish, when shifting to reported speech, we change verb tenses (present to past, etc.) and pronouns, but keep the basic sentence structure. In Arabic, the transformation is more radical: in addition to changing tenses (which in Arabic are based on aspect rather than absolute time), you must handle the particle 'أن' and the declension of nouns according to their function. A common mistake is to translate 'he said that' literally as 'قال أن', but in Modern Standard Arabic, 'أن' is often omitted and the verb is placed in the subjunctive (منصوب) after 'أن' if used. The key: in Arabic, the verb in the subordinate clause maintains its aspect (perfect or imperfect) according to meaning, and there is no rigid sequence of tenses as in Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, reported speech is typically formed with a speech verb (قال، أخبر، سأل، أجاب) followed by the particle 'أنّ' (that) or 'أنْ' (that + subjunctive), depending on whether the subordinate clause is nominal or verbal. For declarative sentences with verbs in the imperfect, 'أنْ' + subjunctive (منصوب) is used if the verb expresses desire, obligation, or uncertain future; but for certain past facts, 'أنّ' + nominal clause (with subject in nominative) is used. In practice, many constructions omit the particle and simply juxtapose the clause with the verb in perfect (for past) or imperfect (for present/future). Like in Spanish, personal and possessive pronouns change according to the original speaker. Important: in Arabic, there is no 'back-shifting' of tenses as in Spanish (e.g., 'he said he had' → 'قال إنه كان لديه'), but the appropriate aspect is used: perfect for completed actions, imperfect for ongoing or habitual actions. Additionally, indirect questions are introduced with 'هل' (yes/no) or interrogative words (ماذا، أين، متى), and 'si' is not used; instead, 'هل' is used directly.

concept_examples.translation: He said that he would travel tomorrow.
She told me that she had been at home.
He asked me what I wanted to eat.
He answered that he hadn’t seen the movie.

common_error.wrong: قال أن هو ذهب إلى السوق.
common_error.correct_alt: قال إنه قد ذهب إلى السوق.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish we say 'he said that he went', but in Arabic, the particle 'أن' (that) must be 'إنّ' (with kasra) when introducing a nominal clause (subject + predicate). Additionally, the pronoun 'هو' must be a clitic suffix: 'إنه' (innahu). The error arises because Spanish speakers use 'أن' (which in Arabic is for subjunctive) generally, without distinguishing between 'إنّ' (that + nominal clause) and 'أنْ' (that + subjunctive verb). Remember: if the subordinate clause is a nominal sentence with a past verb, use 'إنّ' + pronominal suffix; if it’s a present verb expressing future or desire, use 'أنْ' + subjunctive.

examples.translation: She said that she likes reading (that reading is pleasing to her).
examples.note: The verb 'تحب' is in the imperfect, indicating a habitual action or present state, with no need for tense shifting as in Spanish.

examples.translation: He confirmed that the result had been good.
examples.note: 'أنّ' + nominal clause (النتيجة كانت) with 'كان' in the perfect is translated into Spanish as pluperfect due to the sequence of tenses.

examples.translation: He claimed to know the truth.
examples.note: The imperfect 'يعرف' is maintained because it expresses ongoing knowledge, with no direct equivalent of 'sabía' in Spanish.

examples.translation: He asked me if I had gone to the library.
examples.note: In yes/no indirect questions, 'هل' is used instead of 'si'. The verb remains in the perfect, with no need to shift to pluperfect necessarily.

examples.translation: He told me when he would return from the trip.
examples.note: Indirect questions with interrogative words (متى) are introduced directly without additional particles, and future is expressed with 'سـ' (prefix) which does not change.

examples.translation: I asked where he had put the keys.
examples.note: The verb 'وضع' in the perfect remains unchanged, without shifting to a more distant past tense as in Spanish.

levels.label: أوامر وطلبات منقولة / Órdenes y solicitudes referidas

examples.translation: She asked him to study diligently.
examples.note: After 'طلب' (to ask/request), 'أنْ' + subjunctive verb (يدرسَ) is used to express an order or desire, similar to the subjunctive in Spanish.

examples.translation: He advised me not to travel alone.
examples.note: The negation of 'أنْ' is 'ألا' (that not), and the verb 'أسافر' takes the subjunctive ending (-a). It is equivalent to 'que no + subjunctive' in Spanish.

examples.original: أمر الجنود بأن يهاجموا عند الفجر.
examples.phonetic: ʔamara l-junūda bi-ʔan yahājimū ʕinda l-fajr.
examples.translation: He ordered the soldiers to attack at dawn.
examples.note: After 'أمر' (to order), 'بأنْ' (bi-ʔan) + subjunctive is used; the verb 'يهاجموا' takes the -ū ending in subjunctive for masculine plural.

title: التقديم للتركيز (ليس فقط...، نادراً...) / Inversion for emphasis (no solo..., rarely...)
bridge: In Arabic, when emphasizing a negative or restrictive expression, the order is often inverted by placing the emphasized element at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the verb or the particle 'إنّ'. Unlike Spanish, inversion in Arabic does not always require a change in verb form, but it does involve a syntactic rearrangement that may affect agreement or the use of 'ما' and 'لا'. Be careful: Spanish speakers tend to translate 'no solo' literally as 'ليس فقط', but in Arabic it is common to use 'لا... فحسب' or 'ليس... فحسب' with the corresponding inversion.
rule: To emphasize an element in Arabic, it can be placed at the beginning of the sentence. If the element is a negative or restrictive expression, such as 'ليس فقط' (no solo) or 'نادرًا ما' (rarely), the following structures are used: [emphatic expression + ما + verb] or [emphatic expression + إنّ + subject + predicate]. With 'ليس فقط' (laysa faqaṭ), 'بل' (sino) is typically used to introduce the second element. With 'نادرًا ما' (nādiran mā), the verb is in the past or present tense, and the subject can be omitted if it is clear. For 'لا... ولا' (ni... ni), the negated elements are placed at the beginning. Inversion is mandatory when these expressions start the sentence. Examples: 'ليس فقط يدرس، بل يعمل' (No solo estudia, sino que trabaja). 'نادرًا ما نذهب إلى البحر' (Raramente vamos al mar). 'لا أصدقاء ولا عائلة' (Ni amigos ni familia). The particle 'ما' can also be used for emphasis with verbs: 'ما زال يدرس' (Aún estudia).

concept_examples.text: ليس فقط يدرس، بل يعمل أيضًا.
concept_examples.translation: No solo estudia, sino que también trabaja.
concept_examples.phonetic: laysa faqaṭ yadrusu, bal yaʿmal aydan.

concept_examples.translation: Raramente viajamos en invierno.

concept_examples.text: لا مال ولا جاه ينفع في الآخرة.
concept_examples.translation: Ni dinero ni posición sirven en la otra vida.
concept_examples.phonetic: lā māl wa-lā jāh yanfaʿu fī al-ākhira.

concept_examples.translation: Ciertamente, el conocimiento tiene un gran valor.

common_error.wrong: ليس فقط يدرس، لكن يعمل. (traducción literal de 'no solo estudia, pero trabaja')
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we use 'pero' after 'no solo', but in Arabic the correct conjunction is 'بل' (sino), which introduces a complementary or contrasting idea. 'لكن' (pero) is used for strong contrast, not for this emphatic structure. To avoid the error, remember that 'بل' is the fixed form after 'ليس فقط' or 'لا... فحسب'.

examples.original: ليس فقط يتكلم العربية، بل يكتبها بطلاقة.
examples.phonetic: laysa faqaṭ yatakallamu al-ʿarabiyya, bal yaktubuhā bi-ṭalāqa.
examples.translation: No solo habla árabe, sino que lo escribe con fluidez.
examples.note: Observa que después de 'ليس فقط' el verbo va en presente y luego 'بل' introduce el segundo acto.

examples.original: ليس فقط في المدرسة، بل في البيت أيضًا.
examples.phonetic: laysa faqaṭ fī al-madrasa, bal fī al-bayt aydan.
examples.translation: No solo en la escuela, sino también en casa.
examples.note: Aquí se enfatizan lugares, y 'أيضًا' (también) se coloca al final para reforzar.

examples.translation: No se conformó con aprobar, sino que sobresalió.
examples.note: En esta variante, 'لم يكتفِ' (no se conformó) es otra forma de expresar 'no solo', seguida de 'بل'.

examples.translation: Raramente llego tarde al trabajo.
examples.note: 'نادرًا ما' va seguido del verbo en presente: estructura fija.

examples.translation: Raramente nos visitan los parientes.
examples.note: El verbo va después de 'ما' y el sujeto puede aparecer después del verbo.

examples.original: نادرًا ما كانت السماء صافية في الشتاء.
examples.phonetic: nādiran mā kānat al-samāʾ ṣāfiya fī al-shitāʾ.
examples.translation: Raramente el cielo estaba despejado en invierno.
examples.note: Con verbos en pasado, 'ما' se coloca antes del verbo auxiliar 'كانت'.

examples.original: لا في البيت ولا في العمل أشعر بالراحة.
examples.phonetic: lā fī al-bayt wa-lā fī al-ʿamal ashʿuru bil-rāḥa.
examples.translation: Ni en casa ni en el trabajo me siento cómodo.
examples.note: Los elementos negados se colocan al inicio, y el verbo y el sujeto van al final.

examples.original: لا خوفٌ ولا حزنٌ يمنعنا من المضي قدمًا.
examples.phonetic: lā khawf wa-lā ḥuzn yamnaʿunā min al-muḍī qadaman.
examples.translation: Ni miedo ni tristeza nos impiden avanzar.
examples.note: El verbo concuerda en singular con el primer elemento, pero puede ser plural según el sentido.

title: التركيبات الموصولة (It is/was... that) / Split Constructions (It is/was... that)
bridge: In Spanish, to emphasize an element of the sentence, we use constructions like 'Fue Juan quien lo hizo' (It was Juan who did it) or 'Es ahora cuando importa' (It is now when it matters). In Arabic, this function is mainly achieved through the particle إنّما (innamā) or the structure 'ma ... illā' (ما...إلاّ), which expresses exclusion or restriction. Unlike Spanish, where the verb 'ser' appears explicitly, in Arabic it is often omitted or replaced by particles that already incorporate the emphasis. A common mistake is to translate 'es...que' literally using كان (kāna) excessively, when the natural structure is different.
rule:
In Arabic, cleft constructions are formed mainly in two ways:
1) With إنّما (innamā) at the beginning of the sentence: إنّما + [emphasized element] + [rest of the sentence]. Example: إنّما زيدٌ يكتبُ (Innamā Zaydun yaktubu) = 'It is Zaid who writes'.
2) With the negative-exclusive structure: ما + [element] + إلاّ + [complement]. Example: ما زيدٌ إلاّ كاتبٌ (Mā Zaydun illā kātibun) = 'Zaid is nothing but a writer' or 'Zaid is only a writer'. This structure does not have an exact equivalent in Spanish, but it serves to emphasize that only the mentioned element fulfills the condition.
Kāna (كان) can also be used to emphasize time or place, though it is less common: كان في المدرسةِ أنْ التقيتُ به (Kāna fī l-madrasati an iltaqaytu bihi) = 'It was at school where I met him'. In this case, the relative clause is introduced with أنْ (an) or the relative pronoun الذي (alladhī) depending on the context.
Typical uses include: answering questions with emphasis, correcting an assumption, or highlighting a specific element (person, thing, time, place). For B2 level, it is important to distinguish between إنّما (more formal, introduces the whole sentence) and ما...إلاّ (more colloquial and versatile).

concept_examples.text: إنّما الصبرُ على البلاءِ يجزى به الجنةُ.
concept_examples.translation: It is patience in the face of trials that is rewarded with paradise.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʾinnamā ṣ-ṣabru ʿalā l-balāʾi yujzā bihi l-jannatu.

concept_examples.translation: I am nothing but an ordinary student / I am just an ordinary student.

concept_examples.text: كان في القاهرةِ أنْ رأيتُ الهرمَ.
concept_examples.translation: It was in Cairo where I saw the pyramid.
concept_examples.phonetic: kāna fī l-qāhirati ʾan raʾaytu l-harama.

common_error.wrong: كان هو الذي ذهب إلى السوق.
common_error.correct_alt: ما ذهبَ إلى السوقِ إلاّ هوَ.
common_error.explanation: The error comes from translating 'it was he who went to the market' literally using 'kāna' + relative pronoun. While this structure is not incorrect in all contexts, it sounds artificial and unnatural in Modern Standard Arabic. The most idiomatic way is to use 'innamā' or 'mā...illā' to emphasize the subject. Avoid translating 'it is...that' directly; instead, place the emphasized element after the particle.

examples.translation: It is knowledge that is a light (knowledge is what is a light).
examples.note: Here innamā emphasizes that knowledge is solely light, nothing else.

examples.translation: It is brotherhood that the believers are.
examples.note: The structure innamā + subject + nominal predicate.

examples.original: إنّما يخشى اللهَ من عباده العلماءُ.
examples.phonetic: ʾinnamā yakhshā llāha min ʿibādihi l-ʿulamāʾu.
examples.translation: It is only the scholars among His servants who fear Allah.
examples.note: In this example, innamā emphasizes that fear of Allah is exclusive to the scholars.

examples.translation: No one left except Zaid (only Zaid left).
examples.note: Emphasizes that no one else left except Zaid.

examples.translation: I saw nothing but a book (I only saw a book).
examples.note: The emphasis falls on the direct object.

examples.translation: This is nothing but a dream.
examples.note: Fixed structure to deny identity and affirm something exclusively.

levels.label: كان للتوكيد الزمني والمكاني
levels.translation: Kāna for temporal and locative emphasis

examples.translation: It was in the morning when he traveled.
examples.note: Kāna is used to emphasize time, followed by the particle an.

examples.original: كان من الجبلِ أنْ رأيتُ المدينةَ.
examples.phonetic: kāna mina l-jabali ʾan raʾaytu l-madīnata.
examples.translation: It was from the mountain where I saw the city.
examples.note: Emphasis on the place of origin.

examples.original: كان في الماءِ أنْ وجدَ الطفلُ.
examples.phonetic: kāna fī l-māʾi ʾan wajada ṭ-ṭiflu.
examples.translation: It was in the water where the child found it.
examples.note: Use in narrative context.

title: الاسمية (تحويل الأفعال والصفات إلى أسماء) / Nominalization
bridge: In Arabic, nominalization is typically done through the 'masdar' (مصدر), which is the verbal noun, and through derivational patterns for adjectives and other nouns. A common mistake is translating Spanish structures literally, using verbs where Arabic uses nouns, or vice versa. Additionally, in Arabic the verbal noun (masdar) is a central category that functions as an infinitive and as an action noun, something that has no direct equivalent in Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, nominalization is primarily achieved through the 'masdar' (مصدر), which is the verbal noun, and through derivational patterns for adjectives and other nouns. For Form I (ثلاثي مجرد) verbs, the masdar usually follows patterns like فَعْل (e.g. كَتْب), فِعَال (e.g. كِتاب), or فُعُول (e.g. سُجُود). For derived verb forms (II-X), the masdar follows fixed patterns: Form II → تَفْعِيل (e.g. تَدْرِيب), Form III → مُفَاعَلَة (e.g. مُشَارَكَة), Form IV → إِفْعَال (e.g. إِكْرَام), Form V → تَفَعُّل (e.g. تَعَلُّم), Form VI → تَفَاعُل (e.g. تَعَاوُن), Form VII → اِنْفِعَال (e.g. اِنْكِسَار), Form VIII → اِفْتِعَال (e.g. اِجْتِمَاع), Form IX → اِفْعِلَال (e.g. اِحْمِرَار), Form X → اِسْتِفْعَال (e.g. اِسْتِخْدَام). For adjectives, abstract nouns can be formed using the pattern فَعَالَة (e.g. صَدَاقَة from صَدِيق) or فُعُولَة (e.g. سُهُولَة from سَهْل), though for quality adjectives the pattern فِعَالَة is used (e.g. كِذْبَة from كَاذِب). Additionally, place and time nouns follow patterns like مَفْعَل / مَفْعِل (e.g. مَكْتَب, مَوْعِد). The choice of the correct pattern is often not predictable for Form I; it must be memorized. There are also masdars of verbs with hamza and reduplication, with special patterns (e.g. أَكْل, أَمْر). At B2 level, students are expected to recognize and use masdars of derived forms fluently, and to know how to form nouns from common adjectives.

concept_examples.translation: Education is important for society.
I like reading in my free time.

concept_examples.text: اِسْتِخْدَامُ التِّكْنُولُوجْيَا فِي التَّعْلِيمِ أَمْرٌ ضَرُورِيٌّ.
concept_examples.translation: The use of technology in education is a necessity.
concept_examples.phonetic: istiχˈdaːmu t-tiknuːˈluːdʒjaː fiː t-taʕˈliːmi ʔamrun dˤaruːˈrijj

concept_examples.translation: He has the ability to listen well.

common_error.explanation: A common error is using the construction with أَنْ + subjunctive verb when in Arabic it is preferable or even obligatory to use the masdar in nominalization contexts, especially after verbs like 'to like', 'to love', or 'to prefer'. In Spanish, the infinitive is used ('me gusta leer'), but in Arabic the masdar is more formal and frequent. Another correct variant is to keep أَنْ + verb, but the declension of the object must be carefully observed (the ending -a in الكُتُبَ, not -i). To avoid this error, identify whether the main verb governs a masdar or a subordinate clause with أَنْ; in most cases, the masdar is the most natural and concise option.

levels.label: مَصْدَرُ الفِعْلِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ
levels.translation: Masdar of the triliteral verb (Form I)

examples.translation: Reading books increases knowledge.
examples.note: The masdar of قَرَأَ is قِرَاءَة, following the pattern فِعَالَة. It is very common and used as a noun.

examples.translation: Drinking water is necessary for life.
examples.note: The masdar of شَرِبَ is شُرْب, following the pattern فَعْل. Often the masdar of Form I is not predictable; it must be memorized.

examples.translation: Writing the letter takes time.
examples.note: The masdar of كَتَبَ is كِتَابَة, following the same pattern فِعَالَة. Note that it is used here as the subject.

examples.translation: Learning the language requires patience.
examples.note: Form V (تَعَلَّمَ) has the masdar تَعَلُّم, following the pattern تَفَعُّل. It is common in learning contexts.

examples.translation: The participation of students in activities is important.
examples.note: Form III (شَارَكَ) has the masdar مُشَارَكَة, following the pattern مُفَاعَلَة. Note that this pattern is very regular.

examples.translation: Extracting oil requires high technology.
examples.note: Form X (اِسْتَخْرَجَ) has the masdar اِسْتِخْرَاج, following the pattern اِسْتِفْعَال. It is a very productive pattern for verbs of obtaining.

levels.label: تَحْوِيلُ الصِّفَاتِ إِلَى أَسْمَاءٍ
levels.translation: Conversion of adjectives to abstract nouns

examples.translation: Freedom is a fundamental right.
examples.note: From حُرّ (free) comes حُرِّيَّة following the pattern فُعْلِيَّة. This pattern is common for qualities.

examples.translation: Safety is more important than speed.
examples.note: From سَالِم (healthy) comes سَلَامَة, following the pattern فَعَالَة. It is common for states or qualities.

examples.translation: Beauty lies in the eyes.

title: أفعال ناقصة متقدمة / Advanced Modals (would have done, should have done…)
bridge: In Spanish, compound modals like 'habría hecho' or 'debería haber hecho' are formed with the compound conditional and the infinitive of the main verb. In Arabic, there is no direct equivalent of modal verbs with compound tenses; instead, specific particles and verb forms are used, such as «كانَ» (kāna) conjugated in the past or present, combined with the main verb in the subjunctive or jussive mood. The key difference is that Arabic expresses conditionality and reproach through combinations like «كان» + «سوف» or «لم» + the verb in the jussive, which can be confusing for Spanish speakers seeking parallel structures. Additionally, negation and deontic modality (obligation) have distinct nuances: in Arabic, «يجب أن» is used for obligation, but for past reproaches, «كان يجب أن» or «كان ينبغي أن» are preferred.
rule:
In Arabic, to express advanced modals like 'would have done' (compound conditional) or 'should have done' (should + compound infinitive), several strategies are used:

1) Compound conditional (would have + past participle): It is constructed with the particle «كان» (kāna) in the past (to indicate unreal condition) followed by «سَـ» (sa-) or «سوف» (sawfa) and a verb in the imperfect (indicative), or with «كان» + verb in the preterite. Example: «كنت سأفعل» (kuntu sa-afʿal) = 'I would have done' (lit. 'I was + I will do'). «لو» (law) is also used for unreal conditions in conditional sentences.

2) Should have + past participle (reproach or unfulfilled obligation): «كان يجب أن» (kāna yajibu an) or «كان ينبغي أن» (kāna yanbaghī an) are used followed by a verb in the subjunctive (indicative after أن). Example: «كان يجب أن تذهب» (kāna yajibu an taḏhaba) = 'you should have gone'.

3) Negation of compound modals: To negate 'would not have done', «لما كان» (lamā kāna) or «ما كان» (mā kāna) + verb in the imperfect is used, but it is more common to use «لم» + verb in the jussive in conditional contexts. Example: «لم أكن سأفعل» (lam akun sa-afʿal) = 'I would not have done'.

4) Nuances: Arabic differentiates between ability (يمكن أن yumkinu an), possibility (قد qad + verb), necessity (يجب أن yajibu an), and desire (أتمنى أن atamannā an). At the B2 level, it is crucial to recognize that modals are not combined with compound tenses as in Spanish; instead, temporality is marked in the auxiliary «كان» and the modal nuance in the particle or modal verb.

Exceptions: In Modern Standard Arabic, «كان من الممكن أن» (kāna min al-mumkin an) is sometimes used for 'it would have been possible that', and «كان يجب أن» for reproaches. In dialects, there are variations, but this concept focuses on Standard Arabic.

concept_examples.translation: If I had known, I would have come.
You should have studied more.

concept_examples.text: كان يمكن أن ينجح لو حاول.
concept_examples.translation: He could have succeeded if he had tried.
concept_examples.phonetic: kāna yumkinu an yanjaha law ḥāwala.

concept_examples.text: لم أكن سأفعل ذلك لو كنت مكانك.
concept_examples.translation: I wouldn’t have done that if I were in your place.
concept_examples.phonetic: lam akun sa-afʿal dhālika law kuntu makānak.

common_error.wrong: يجب أن ذهبت (incorrect: 'should have gone' as if using direct past)
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because the Spanish speaker attempts a literal translation of 'should have gone' using 'يجب أن' (should) + past tense verb, but in Arabic the structure requires the auxiliary «كان» in the past to indicate that the obligation was not fulfilled, followed by «أن» + verb in the subjunctive (present). The correct form is «كان يجب أن» + verb in the present (subjunctive), since the past temporal reference is marked in «كان».

examples.translation: If I were in your place, I would have gone there.
examples.note: «لو» + past is used for the condition, and «لَـ» (la) + past for the result.

examples.translation: If I had had time, I would have traveled.
examples.note: Note that «كان» agrees with the subject, and the result takes «لَـ».

examples.translation: If I had studied, I would have passed.
examples.note: «لو أنني» (if I) can be used for emphasis.

examples.translation: You should have called us.
examples.note: «كان يجب أن» + verb in the subjunctive (present) is used.

examples.translation: I should have told the truth.
examples.note: «ينبغي» is a formal synonym of «يجب».

examples.translation: It would have been better if you had waited.
examples.note: Alternative to suggest a better option.

levels.label: التعبير عن الاحتمال والإمكانية في الماضي
levels.translation: Expressing past probability and possibility (could have)

examples.translation: You could have won the match.
examples.note: «كان يمكن أن» + subjunctive expresses past possibility not realized.

examples.original: قد كان يمكن أن نصل مبكراً لو لم نضل الطريق.
examples.phonetic: qad kāna yumkinu an naṣila mubakkiran law lam naḍil al-ṭarīq.
examples.translation: We could have arrived early if we hadn’t gotten lost.
examples.note: Adding «قَد» emphasizes possibility and combines with «لو» for the condition.

examples.original: كان من الممكن أن يكون الجو أفضل اليوم.
examples.phonetic: kāna min al-mumkin an yakūna al-jaww afḍal al-yawm.
examples.translation: The weather could have been better today.
examples.note: «من الممكن أن» is another way to express possibility, equivalent to «يمكن أن».

title: الجمل الفعلية / Clauses of circumstance
bridge: In Spanish, we often use participle clauses ('caminando por la calle, vi...') to express simultaneous actions or circumstances. In Arabic, this construction does not exist in the same way: Arabic uses the 'حال' (ḥāl) form, which is a subordinate clause introduced by 'و' (wa) and often with an explicit pronoun. Additionally, the active participle (اسم الفاعل) can be used with adverbial value, but its use is more limited than in Spanish. The main trick is that Spanish speakers tend to translate 'caminando' literally as a gerund, but in Arabic the structure with 'و' or the active participle in specific cases must be used.
rule: In Arabic, to express a circumstance or simultaneous action (equivalent to Spanish participle clauses), the construction called 'حال' (ḥāl) is used. This can be: 1) A verbal sentence introduced by 'و' (wa) followed by a subject and a verb in the present or past tense, always with an explicit pronoun referring to the main subject. Example: 'دخلتُ والكلبُ ينبحُ' (I entered and the dog was barking). 2) An active participle (اسم الفاعل) in the accusative case (حال مفرد), functioning as an adverb, for example: 'جاء مسرعًا' (he came running). 3) It can also be a nominal sentence without 'و' when the subject is the same. At B2 level, mastery of structures with 'و' and the active participle in the accusative case is expected. Care must be taken with gender and number agreement, and with the accusative case of the participle. The gerund is not used as in Spanish.

concept_examples.translation: He walked down the street singing.
I entered the office, with the manager sitting.
She came running to the house.
I read the book standing.

common_error.correct_alt: بينما كنتُ أمشي في الشارعِ، رأيتُ صديقي.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, the participle clause is juxtaposed without a connector ('caminando por la calle, vi a mi amigo'). When translating into Arabic, Spanish speakers often omit the particle 'و' (wa) that introduces the حال clause. In Arabic, simultaneity is marked with 'و' before the subordinate clause. It is also common to use 'بينما' (while) as an alternative. Remember that the verb in the حال clause is usually in the present or past tense, and the subject must be explicit.

levels.label: الحال المفردة / Active participle as adverb
levels.translation: The active participle functioning as an adverb

examples.translation: The man entered laughing.
examples.note: The active participle 'ضاحكًا' is in the accusative case (with tanwin -an) and agrees in gender and number with the subject. Here it indicates the circumstance of the main action.

examples.translation: She left crying.
examples.note: The feminine participle 'باكيةً' is used in the accusative. In Spanish we use the gerund, but in Arabic it is an active participle.

examples.translation: He looked at me smiling.
examples.note: When the participle is derived from a verb with more than three letters, like 'ابتسم' (to smile), the active participle of the same root is used.

levels.label: الحال الجملة الفعلية مع و / Circumstance with verbal sentence introduced by 'wa'
levels.translation: Circumstance expressed with a verbal sentence introduced by 'wa'

examples.translation: I entered the office, the employees working.
examples.note: The subordinate clause 'والموظفون يعملون' begins with 'و' (wa) and has an explicit subject and a verb in the present tense.

examples.translation: We left the house, raining.
examples.note: Here the حال clause describes an external circumstance. The verb 'يهطل' is in the present tense, indicating simultaneity with the main action.

examples.translation: I heard the news with my heart pounding.
examples.note: The حال clause can express an emotion or physical state. The subject 'قلبي' is different from the main subject.

levels.label: الحال الجملة الاسمية / Circumstance with nominal sentence introduced by 'wa'
levels.translation: Circumstance expressed with a nominal sentence introduced by 'wa'

examples.translation: I entered the hall, the audience being silent.
examples.note: The nominal sentence 'والجمهور ساكن' uses a noun and an adjective/predicate. The predicate can be an adjective or an active participle.

examples.translation: We traveled with good weather.
examples.note: This structure is equivalent to an adverbial clause of manner in Spanish. It is used to describe the state in which the action occurs.

examples.translation: He sat on the chair with his head bowed.
examples.note: The predicate of the nominal sentence can be an active participle with an adjective form, such as 'منحنٍ' (bowed).

title: صيغة المضارع المنصوب (الفعل بعد أنْ المشروطة) – «Formal Subjunctive»
bridge: In Arabic, there is a verb form similar to the subjunctive called المضارع المنصوب (present subjunctive), used after particles like أنْ (that), لِـ (in order to), حتى (so that), and others. The main challenge is that the final vowel changes (from -u to -a), and in defective verbs, the last letter is often dropped. Additionally, negation in the subjunctive is done with لا (no) rather than ما as in the indicative. Note that there isn’t always a direct equivalence with Spanish: sometimes Arabic uses the indicative where Spanish requires the subjunctive, and vice versa.
rule:
The المضارع المنصوب (present subjunctive) in Arabic is used after particles such as: أنْ (that), لِـ (in order to), حتى (so that), كي (so that), لن (will not + future subjunctive). Formation depends on the verb type: 
- Sound verbs (no weakness): marked with a fatḥa (a) on the last letter: يَكْتُبُ → يَكْتُبَ (that he writes). 
- Defective verbs (ending in ا, و, or ي): the last letter is dropped. Example: يَرْجُو (he hopes) → يَرْجُوَ (that he hopes). 
Negation: لن + المضارع المنصوب (future negative) – example: لَنْ يَكْتُبَ (he will not write). 
Common usage: after expressions like من الضروري أن (it is essential that), من المهم أن (it is important that), يجب أن (it must be that).

concept_examples.translation: It is essential that you study diligently.
We must respect the country's laws.

concept_examples.text: لَنْ أُصَدِّقَ أَيَّ شَيْءٍ قَبْلَ التَّأَكُّدِ.
concept_examples.translation: I will not believe anything before verifying.
I want him to go to the doctor.

common_error.explanation: The most common mistake is keeping the indicative vowel (ḍamma /u/) instead of the subjunctive one (fatḥa /a/). In Spanish, the subjunctive is marked by a different verbal ending (estudies vs. estudias), but in Arabic, the distinction is only in the vowel, which is hard for Spanish speakers to perceive. Remember: after أنْ, the last letter of the verb must carry a fatḥa (a).

levels.label: أنْ بعد أفعال الإرادة والرغبة
levels.translation: أنْ after verbs of will and desire

examples.original: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَسْكُنَ فِي مَدِينَةٍ هَادِئَةٍ.
examples.translation: I want to live in a quiet city.
examples.note: The verb أَسْكُنَ ends with a fatḥa because it follows أنْ.

examples.original: يَرْغَبُ الطُّلَّابُ أَنْ يَتَعَلَّمُوا اللُّغَةَ العَرَبِيَّةَ.
examples.translation: The students wish to learn the Arabic language.
examples.note: The verb يَتَعَلَّمُوا ends in واو (as it is plural) and does not change, but it is considered correct in the subjunctive.

levels.label: أنْ بعد التعبيرات الشرطية والضرورية
levels.translation: أنْ after expressions of necessity and condition

examples.original: مِنَ المُهِمِّ أَنْ تَحْضُرَ فِي الوَقْتِ.
examples.translation: It is important that you arrive on time.
examples.note: The expression مِنَ المُهِمِّ (it is important) requires the subjunctive in the subordinate clause.

examples.original: لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَعْمَلَ الجَمِيعُ بِجِدٍّ.
examples.translation: It is essential that everyone work diligently.
examples.note: لَا بُدَّ أَنْ means 'it is inevitable that' and is followed by the subjunctive.

examples.translation: We will not forget the sacrifices of our ancestors.
examples.note: لَنْ causes the verb نَنْسَى to become نَنْسَ (a defective verb loses its final letter in this context).

examples.translation: I will not accept this treatment.
examples.note: The verb أَقْبَلَ ends with a fatḥa due to لن.

title: المستقبل التام والمستقبل المستمر / Future Perfect and Future Continuous
bridge: In Arabic, there are no compound verb forms equivalent to the Spanish future perfect and future continuous. Instead, particles like سَـ (sa-) or سَوْفَ (sawfa) are used with the present tense verb, and the continuous or perfect aspect is inferred from context or expressed with additional constructions. The main challenge for Spanish speakers is that Arabic does not mark aspect in the same way, so learners must use time adverbs and modal particles to convey the same idea. Additionally, Arabic lacks an auxiliary verb for 'haber' or an equivalent to the compound past participle, requiring a shift in mental perspective.
rule: In Arabic, the future is formed with the prefix سَـ (sa-) or the particle سَوْفَ (sawfa) before the present tense verb (المضارع). To express the future continuous, the same construction is used, and context or adverbs like 'في ذلك الوقت' (at that time) indicate the action is ongoing. For the future perfect, the construction 'سيكون قد + فعل ماضٍ' (sakuuna qad + past verb) is used, which literally means 'it will be that [subject] has already done something.' This is the most common way to indicate that an action will be completed at a future point. For the future continuous, 'سيكون + اسم فاعل' (sakuunu + active participle) can be used, or simply the present tense with future meaning. Time adverbs such as 'بحلول' (by the time), 'في السنة القادمة' (next year), and 'حتى ذلك الحين' (until then) are essential for clarifying aspect. It is important to remember that Arabic does not have an auxiliary verb like 'haber,' and the future perfect is constructed with 'كان' (to be) in the future tense and the particle 'قَد' (already) with a past verb.

concept_examples.text: سَأَكُونُ قَدِ انْتَهَيْتُ مِنْ عَمَلِي بِحُلُولِ السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ.
concept_examples.translation: Habré terminado mi trabajo para las cinco.
concept_examples.phonetic: saʔakuːnu qadi intahajtu min ʕamalī biḥulūli as-sāʕati al-xāmisah.

concept_examples.text: سَوْفَ أَكُونُ أَعْمَلُ فِي الْمَكْتَبِ غَدًا فِي هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ.
concept_examples.translation: Estaré trabajando en la oficina mañana a esta hora.
concept_examples.phonetic: sawfa ʔakuːnu ʔaʕmalu fī al-maktabi ġadan fī hāḏā al-waqt.

concept_examples.text: بِحُلُولِ نِهَايَةِ الْعَامِ، سَأَكُونُ قَدْ زُرْتُ ثَلَاثَ دُوَلٍ.
concept_examples.translation: Para fin de año, habré visitado tres países.
concept_examples.phonetic: biḥulūli nihāyati al-ʕāmi, saʔakuːnu qad zurtu ṯalāṯa duwalin.

concept_examples.text: عِنْدَمَا تَصِلُ، سَأَكُونُ أَنْتَظِرُكَ فِي الْمُطَارِ.
concept_examples.translation: Cuando llegues, te estaré esperando en el aeropuerto.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʕindamā taṣilu, saʔakuːnu ʔantaẓiruka fī al-muṭāri.

common_error.correct: سَوْفَ أَكُونُ قَدِ انْتَهَيْتُ مِنْ عَمَلِي.
common_error.explanation: A common mistake is omitting the particle 'قَد' (already) when using 'يكون' in the future to express the future perfect. In Spanish, 'habré terminado' is formed with an auxiliary + past participle, and when translating literally, Spanish speakers tend to omit 'قَد,' which is the particle introducing the past verb to indicate a completed action. Without 'قَد,' the phrase means 'I will be finished' (which is incoherent). Always add 'قَد' after 'يكون' in the future to form the future perfect.

levels.label: تَكْوِينُ الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ التَّامِّ / Formation of the Future Perfect

examples.translation: Habré comido antes de que llegues.
examples.note: This structure uses 'سَأَكُونُ' (I will be) + 'قَدْ' (already) + past verb. It is the standard way to indicate a completed future action.

examples.original: بِحُلُولِ الْعَاشِرَةِ، سَيَكُونُونَ قَدْ غَادَرُوا الْمَنْزِلَ.
examples.phonetic: biḥulūli al-ʕāširah, sayakūnūna qad ġādarū al-manzila.
examples.translation: Para las diez, habrán salido de casa.
examples.note: The masculine plural ending 'ونَ' in 'سَيَكُونُونَ' agrees with the plural subject.

examples.original: لَنْ أَكُونَ قَدِ اشْتَرَيْتُ السَّيَّارَةَ بَعْدُ.
examples.phonetic: lan ʔakūna qadi štaraytu as-sayyārata baʕdu.
examples.translation: No habré comprado el coche todavía.
examples.note: With the negative particle 'لَنْ' (not), the subjunctive is used after 'سَيَكُونُ,' here 'أَكُونَ' instead of 'أَكُونُ'.

levels.label: تَكْوِينُ الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ الْمُسْتَمِرِّ / Formation of the Future Continuous

examples.original: سَوْفَ أَكُونُ أَقْرَأُ كِتَابًا فِي الْمَشْرَبِ.
examples.phonetic: sawfa ʔakuːnu ʔaqraʔu kitāban fī al-mašrabi.
examples.translation: Estaré leyendo un libro en la cafetería.
examples.note: The future continuous is formed with 'سَوْفَ أَكُونُ' + present tense verb. It is important not to use 'قَدْ' because the action is not completed.

examples.original: غَدًا فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّحْظَةِ، سَتَكُونُ تَتَمَشَّى فِي الْحَدِيقَةِ.
examples.phonetic: ġadan fī hāḏihi al-laḥẓati, satakūnu tatamaššā fī al-ḥadīqah.
examples.translation: Mañana a esta hora, estarás paseando por el parque.
examples.note: The verb 'تَتَمَشَّى' agrees with 'أَنْتَ' (you) and is used in the present tense to express the ongoing action.

examples.original: عِنْدَمَا تَصِلُ، سَوْفَ يَكُونُ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى التِّلْفَازِ.
examples.phonetic: ʕindamā taṣilu, sawfa yakūnu yanẓuru ʔilā at-tilfāzi.
examples.translation: Cuando llegues, él estará viendo la televisión.
examples.note: The verb 'يَنْظُرُ' (to look) is in the present tense, and the prefix 'يَ-' indicates third-person masculine singular.

levels.label: الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ التَّامِّ وَالْمُسْتَمِرِّ فِي السِّيَاقِ / Contextual Use of Both Tenses

examples.original: سَأَكُونُ قَدِ انْتَهَيْتُ مِنَ الْعَمَلِ، ثُمَّ سَأَكُونُ أَسْتَرِيحُ.
examples.phonetic: saʔakuːnu qadi ntahaytu mina al-ʕamali, ṯumma saʔakuːnu ʔastarīḥu.
examples.translation: Habré terminado el trabajo y luego estaré descansando.
examples.note: The future perfect (completed action) and future continuous (ongoing action) are combined here. The temporal order is indicated with 'ثُمَّ' (then).

examples.original: بِحُلُولِ السَّنَةِ الْمُقْبِلَةِ، سَأَكُونُ قَدْ تَعَلَّمْتُ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ وَسَأَكُونُ أَتَحَدَّثُ بِهَا بِطَلَاقَةٍ.
examples.phonetic: biḥulūli as-sanati al-muqbilati, saʔakuːnu qad taʕallamtu al-luġata al-ʕarabiyyata wa saʔakuːnu ʔataḥaddaṯu bihā biṭalāqah.
examples.translation: Para el año que viene, habré aprendido árabe y estaré hablándolo con fluidez.
examples.note: This example shows the combination of both forms to express two different future actions: one completed and one ongoing.

examples.original: لَنْ تَكُونَ قَدْ أَكَلْتَ حَتَّى أَصِلَ؟
examples.phonetic: lan takūna qad ʔakalta ḥattā ʔaṣila?
examples.translation: ¿No habrás comido hasta que llegue?
examples.note: In negative questions, 'لَنْ' + subjunctive 'تَكُونَ' + 'قَدْ' + past verb is used. The context indicates doubt about a completed future action.
